title: CPU Scheduling
subtitle: Preemptive vs Non-Preemptive scheduling, metrics, criteria, and FCFS mathematical walkthrough.

sections.title: Types of CPU Scheduling
sections.description: CPU scheduling algorithms fall into two broad categories based on whether a running process can be forcefully interrupted.

categories.description: The operating system can forcefully pause a currently running process and allocate the CPU to another process.
Once the CPU has been allocated to a process, the process keeps the CPU until it voluntarily releases it (either by terminating or switching to I/O).

sections.title: Key Timings in CPU Scheduling
sections.description: Essential time parameters used to evaluate and calculate scheduling algorithm performance.

metrics.name: Arrival Time (AT)
metrics.definition: The exact time at which a process enters the ready queue and is ready for execution.

metrics.name: Burst Time / Execution Time (BT)
metrics.definition: The total amount of CPU time required by a process to complete its execution.

metrics.name: Completion Time (CT)
metrics.definition: The time instant at which a process completes its execution and finishes.

metrics.name: Turnaround Time (TAT)
metrics.definition: Total time taken from the moment a process arrives to the time it completes. Formula: TAT = Completion Time - Arrival Time.

metrics.name: Waiting Time (WT)
metrics.definition: Total amount of time a process spends waiting in the ready queue. Formula: WT = Turnaround Time - Burst Time.

metrics.name: Response Time (RT)
metrics.definition: The time elapsed from when a process is submitted until the first time it gets the CPU.

sections.title: CPU Scheduling Criteria & Optimization Goals
general_criteria: CPU Utilization: Keep the CPU as busy as possible.
Throughput: Number of processes completed per time unit.
Turnaround Time (TAT): Total time for process execution.
Waiting Time (WT): Total time spent waiting in ready queue.
Response Time (RT): Time taken to start responding.
sections.why_less_waiting_time_is_good: Lower waiting time means processes spend less idle time in the ready queue, leading to faster user-perceived responsiveness, higher overall system throughput, and optimal resource utilization.

algorithm_optimization_goals.description: Keep hardware processing units active and minimize idle cycles.
Maximize the count of completed processes per unit of time.
Minimize the interval from submission to completion.
Minimize the delay before the first response/execution slice is granted.
